stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HITS 19-YEAR HIGH AS FED HIKE ODDS TOP 92%
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.04% intraday, its highest since July 2007, as the FOMC opened its two-day meeting with CME FedWatch pricing a 92.5% chance of a quarter-point hike Wednesday — the Fed's first hike since 2023. The 2-year yield climbed to 4.66%.
stories.explain: A hike bet this close to certainty means the move is already priced into short-term yields, so the real market risk Wednesday is the dot plot and Powell's language on the pace of further hikes, not the hike itself. Because the Fed is raising into an oil-driven inflation scare rather than an overheating labor market, traders are watching whether officials treat energy costs as transitory or embed them into the forecast — that distinction will move the long end of the curve more than the decision itself.

stories.headline: OIL SPIKES TOWARD FOUR-MONTH HIGH ON MIDDLE EAST SUPPLY SCARE
stories.body: WTI crude jumped 4.0% to $105.49 and Brent pushed near $109 after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline amid the Iran conflict, stripping out a key alternative export route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.explain: The pipeline's role is to let Saudi crude reach the Red Sea without transiting the Strait of Hormuz, so shutting it removes a supply buffer right as tensions raise the odds of a Hormuz disruption — the market is pricing tail risk, not just today's barrel count. That matters for tomorrow's Fed decision because a sustained oil shock is a cost-push input the Fed can't offset with rate policy, forcing officials to choose between tolerating higher headline inflation or hiking into a supply shock that could also slow growth.

stories.headline: STOCKS FALL FOR SECOND STRAIGHT DAY AS SEMICONDUCTORS LEAD DECLINE
stories.body: The S&P 500 slid 0.45% to 7,585.73 and the Dow lost 328 points (-0.63%) to 52,093.11, while chip stocks were hit hardest: Lam Research -8.3%, GE Vernova -8.6%, Intel -5.6%, Micron -5.2%, Broadcom -4.8%, and Nvidia -3.4%.
stories.explain: Semiconductor stocks carry some of the highest duration-sensitivity in the index because their valuations lean on distant future earnings, so a spike in the discount rate (the 10-year yield) compresses their present value disproportionately versus the broader market. That's why the Nasdaq 100 is underperforming the S&P 500 today — it's not a chip-specific news event, it's a rates-driven repricing of the sector most exposed to higher-for-longer yields.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIDES TO MULTI-WEEK LOW AS RATE-HIKE BETS FIRM UP
stories.body: Gold fell 1.4% to trade near $4,290, its lowest level in about a month, as the near-certain Fed hike and surging real yields raised the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
stories.explain: Gold pays no interest, so its attractiveness is inversely tied to real yields — when the 10-year nominal yield jumps to 5% and inflation expectations stay contained, the real (inflation-adjusted) return on bonds rises and gold becomes comparatively less attractive to hold. That relationship is why gold is falling even as an oil-driven geopolitical shock unfolds, a scenario where gold's safe-haven bid would normally be expected to kick in.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX RALLIES TO TWO-WEEK HIGH AHEAD OF FOMC
stories.body: The DXY climbed to 99.75 (+0.3%), extending a fourth straight session of gains as traders positioned for the Fed to raise rates while other major central banks hold steady.
stories.explain: A rate hike widens the interest-rate differential in the dollar's favor relative to currencies like the euro and yen, making dollar-denominated assets more attractive on a yield basis and pulling capital toward the U.S. — that's the direct channel behind DXY's climb into the decision. A stronger dollar also acts as a partial offset to the oil shock for U.S. consumers, since crude is priced in dollars and a stronger greenback makes imported barrels marginally cheaper than the headline price move alone suggests.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S FORWARD DONNIE FREEMAN OUT FOR SEASON WITH ACHILLES INJURY
stories.body: Freeman, a key returning piece for St. John's, ruptured his Achilles during a team workout this week and will miss the entire 2026-27 season. Separately, Duke opened Andy Katz's preseason Power 44 at No. 1 for 2026-27.

stories.headline: TRAIL BLAZERS LAND JA MORANT IN TRADE WITH GRIZZLIES
stories.body: Portland acquired former All-Star guard Ja Morant from Memphis in one of the offseason's biggest moves, headlining a summer that also saw the Celtics lock up forward Jordan Walsh on a three-year, $15 million extension.

stories.headline: CHIEFS ROUT BRONCOS AS WEEK 1 TIES SCORING RECORD
stories.body: Kansas City dominated Denver in Week 1 as the league's opening slate tied the Super Bowl-era record for most points scored in a single week. Attention now turns to Week 2, including the Bills christening their new stadium against the Lions.

stories.headline: TEXAS STUNS NO. 1 OHIO STATE WITH 20-POINT COMEBACK
stories.body: Texas erased a 20-point deficit to upset top-ranked Ohio State, with the Longhorns' quarterback leading the rally and delivering in the clutch to hand the Buckeyes their first loss of the season.

deepDive.title: Why an Oil Shock Complicates a Fed That's About to Hike
content: Today's brief has an unusual pairing: crude oil spiking 4% on a Middle East supply scare on the same day the 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007, one day before the Fed is expected to raise rates for the first time since 2023. Those two moves aren't coincidental. Energy shocks and Fed policy interact directly, because oil is one of the few inputs that shows up almost immediately in the inflation data the Fed is legally obligated to respond to. Understanding that transmission mechanism explains why markets are bracing for hawkish language tomorrow even though the rate decision itself is already fully priced.

Oil enters CPI two ways: directly, through the energy component (gasoline, heating oil, natural gas), which makes up roughly 7% of the headline basket, and indirectly, through freight, plastics, fertilizer, and any input that's refined from or transported using petroleum. The direct effect shows up within a month, as retail gas prices track crude futures closely. The indirect effect lags two to four months as businesses pass higher input costs through their supply chains into finished-good prices. That lag is exactly why a supply shock today becomes a live inflation problem for the Fed's outlook well into the winter, not just a one-day headline.

This is a textbook cost-push shock, and it's the hardest kind of inflation for a central bank to manage, because raising rates doesn't fix a pipeline shutdown — it just slows the rest of the economy while the supply constraint runs its course. The 1973 oil embargo is the canonical case: the Fed under Arthur Burns hiked into an oil shock and got stagflation, high inflation and weak growth simultaneously, because rate hikes attack demand while the actual problem was supply. Most people miss that the Fed's preferred gauge, core PCE, strips out food and energy specifically to avoid overreacting to exactly this kind of shock — but headline CPI still matters because it's what shapes the public's inflation expectations.

That tension is precisely what's live in tomorrow's decision. A near-certain hike is already baked into yields, so the market-moving variable is whether Powell's dot plot treats today's oil spike as noise to look through or as a reason to keep hiking into 2027. If officials lean hawkish and cite energy-driven inflation risk, expect the yield curve to stay inverted or flatten further and the dollar to extend its rally, since dollar strength is the closest thing to a natural offset — a stronger dollar makes dollar-priced oil marginally cheaper for U.S. buyers even as the headline barrel price rises.
